cim: How artificial intelligence could potentially wreck a newsroom
cim_eredeti: How artificial intelligence could potentially wreck a newsroom
szoveg_eredeti:
By Victor Ledbetter Jr., November 17, 2026

I know readers have been wary of the advancements artificial intelligence programs have made in the past half-decade, but have you considered how AI has been applied in the journalism field?

Investing in AI could, in theory, be a good thing for the workplace as a tool to generate ideas. In execution, this could potentially go the other way. This could affect the workplace for the worse and encourage AI reliance.

As reporters, we must make sure all the information we collect and relay to readers is as accurate as possible. These AI programs, while somewhat reliable tools, can muddy the waters a bit. They can cite unreliable resources and get vital facts wrong in the process.

The New York Times and The Associated Press have jumped on the opportunity to utilize the technology.

The Associated Press uses a crop of tools to analyze videos and has collaborated with AppliedXL, an AI startup that detects changes in public databases, to analyze data for the federal registry.

The Associated Press states all information generated by AI are reviewed by editorial staff and will go through necessary deity before being published.

This AP article was published two years ago, without a release date. Who knows how much these policies have changed in the past 24 months.

The Times laid out a set of principles regarding AI use in its articles, including using AI to create drafts of headlines and summaries of articles, as well as using machine-learning models to collect and sort data for investigative reporting. The Times said these tasks are done with human oversight and review.

The publication has also stated they don’t use AI for writing articles, as writers are responsible for the work they publish.

According to a University of Maryland study, more than 9% of articles in the United States contained text created by AI as of October 2025.

Mohit Iyyer, computer science associate professor for University of Maryland, has expressed concerns regarding the accuracy of the content collected by these programs.

“As a reader, you generally don’t have a way to know if the news or the opinions are coming from a human or from AI,” Iyyer said.

This could mean many articles from several publishers have been worked on with AI or have been completely AI generated in the past year.

The use of AI in the newsroom is a reflection on journalists in workplaces around the country.

In the article “The human side of AI: The growing risks of ubiquitous use of AI on talent” by Natalie Runyon, the author asks Cornelia C. Walther to detail her thoughts on unchecked AI use and how it can erode human connection, learning and cognitive skills.

Walther focused on how the rapid adoption of this technology is putting pressure on employees, potentially leaving them feeling overwhelmed in the process.

“Unknowingly, we are sliding down the slippery slope of agency decay,” Walther said.

Walther said employees should try and take control of the full capability of AI by investing in it now before we no longer notice what we have lost.

Applying all of this and more to a newsroom could be chaotic. The morale of the journalists would be low. The information they get could potentially be incorrect and the minds we rely on will lose vital critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

It will always be vital to make sure as journalists we utilize the tools available to us to the best of our ability. AI can be a good tool, sure. Yet we must make sure we can do the hard part ourselves and produce our best. Even if this makes the job easier, we should still put in an effort to be better than a machine.
